app.title: A complete image studio,
body: Type a sentence and get a photograph. Change one thing about it without touching the rest. Put the same face in a dozen different scenes. Turn a still into a few seconds of video. It's all here in one window, and none of it is metered — make ten images or ten thousand, the price doesn't move.

Nothing gets uploaded to be processed somewhere else. Your prompts, your references and everything you make stay where the app is running — which is the difference between a tool you can put a client's unreleased work into and one you can't.

Each tab below is a finished workflow, not a pile of settings. The hard parts are already tuned, so the first thing you type comes back looking like something — and when you want the dials, they're right there. Here's what each one does.

cta.title: Ready to unlock more?
cta.body: Upgrades are applied to your key by hand, and it only takes minutes. You keep working while we do it, and the new tabs are there the next time you start the app.

krea_t2i.headline: Type a sentence. Get a photograph.
body: Describe what you want in plain English — no keyword soup, no special syntax, no list of things to avoid. What comes back is full resolution and sharp enough to print.

What sets it apart is that it doesn't look generated. Skin keeps its texture instead of turning to plastic, fabric keeps its weave, and light behaves like light. Generate a batch, keep the one that works, then lock it and make ten more just like it.

Fast drafts, or slow and perfect

krea_v2_t2i.headline: A second artist, with a different eye.
body: Some days you want the photographer. Some days you want the art director who actually reads the brief. This is the second one: give it a paragraph and it keeps every detail in it — the count, the placement, the colour of the third thing on the left — where a shorter attention span quietly drops half of them.

It's also the one to reach for when there are words in the picture. Signage, packaging, a title on a poster: it writes them legibly, instead of producing something that only looks like text from across the room. Slower per image, and worth it when the brief is specific.

blocks.title: Same words, two artists
blocks.body: One prompt, run once in each tab. Watch which one keeps the hand-painted sign, both cyclists, and the corner it was told to put them on.

block.caption: “a corner bookshop, hand-painted sign reading OPEN LATE, two cyclists passing”

blocks.caption: Briefs long enough that most models start forgetting the end of them.

krea_edit.headline: Tell it what to change. It changes only that.
body: Drop in a photograph and type “make it snow”, or “give her a leather jacket”, or “take the car out of the driveway”. You get the same picture back with that one thing different — same face, same pose, same light, same everything you didn't mention.

No masks, no layers, nothing to select. And because the person stays the person, you can keep going: the jacket, then the weather, then the time of day, one instruction at a time. Five edits later it's still the same shot, not a distant cousin of it.

blocks.caption: “put her in a red wool coat, keep everything else”
One photograph, three instructions, the same person in all of them.

krea_v2_edit.headline: The same trick, for the fussier requests.
body: Everything the Edit tab does, with a longer attention span. Ask for two changes at once — “move him to a studio backdrop and warm up the light” — and it does both, instead of doing the first and quietly averaging away the second.

It's also gentler on the detail that repeated editing tends to sand off: hair, jewellery, the pattern on a shirt. Reach for it when the instruction is a sentence rather than a phrase, or when the picture has already been through a few rounds.

blocks.title: Two changes, one sentence
blocks.body: Ask for the background and the lighting in a single breath and get both, in one pass, without the picture drifting away from the person in it.

block.caption: “move him to a studio backdrop and warm the light”

blocks.caption: One source, three complete changes of scene.

krea_inpaint.headline: Paint over what you want gone.
body: For the fixes that are easier to point at than to describe. Brush over the scooter parked in front of the shop, the logo on the shirt, the ex in the holiday photo — say what should be there instead, and it fills it in as though it always was.

Only what you painted changes. Everything outside the stroke comes back exactly as it was, so you can use it on finished work without risking the ninety per cent that was already right. Rough strokes are fine — the edges blend themselves.

blocks.title: Paint it, describe it, done
blocks.body: The middle frame is the brush stroke, exactly as it was drawn — no precision required. The right one is what came back.

block.caption: “remove the parked scooter, continue the wall behind it”

faceswap.headline: One face, every shot in the set.
body: Give it one clear photograph of a face and it carries that person into any other picture, matching the angle, the lighting and the skin tone — so it reads as a photograph of them, not a cut-out pasted on top.

This is what makes a set hang together. Invent a character in the generation tabs, then run twenty scenes through here and the same person is in all of them. Trying it on a whole folder costs you nothing but the time to pick the reference.
highlights: Run a whole set at once

blocks.caption: Four scenes, one person. The reference on the left is the only photograph of them that exists.

flux_t2i.headline: The graphic designer of the bunch.
body: A different engine with different instincts. Where the others reach for photography, this one reaches for design: flat colour, clean shapes, poster layouts, logos, packaging — anything meant to look made rather than taken.

It's also the best of them with lettering. When an idea stalls in another tab — the composition won't come, the type won't read — running it through here often gets it in one, and everything lands in the same gallery either way.
highlights: A second opinion when you're stuck

blocks.caption: Posters, packaging and type — the work that's supposed to look designed.

klein_i2i.headline: Turn a rough idea into a finished picture.
body: Feed it anything — a phone snap, a pencil sketch, a screenshot of a rough 3D layout — say what it should become, and slide one control between “tidy this up” and “start again from this shape”.

Low keeps your composition exactly where you drew it and just makes it look finished. High keeps the layout and repaints everything else. It's the fastest way from the thing in your head, badly drawn, to something you'd actually show someone.

blocks.caption: One pencil sketch, the same prompt, three positions on the slider.

wan_i2v.headline: Give a still picture a few seconds of life.
body: Hand it any image — one you made here or one from your camera roll — describe the movement, and get a short clip back. Steam rising, hair moving, a slow push toward the subject, water doing what water does. The person in the picture stays the person in the picture.

This is the one that usually costs by the second everywhere else. Here it doesn't cost anything at all, and that changes how you use it: make five versions, keep the one that moves right, throw the other four away without a thought.

blocks.note: the clips play as you scroll past

json_batch.headline: Set up a hundred images and go to bed.
body: Line up a whole list of prompts and settings, press start, and walk away. Each one runs in turn and lands in the gallery — and if one trips over itself, the rest carry on without you.
It's the tab that turns a long afternoon into an overnight job: regenerate an entire shoot after changing one word, or work through every variation of an idea while you're doing something else.
highlights: Queue as many as you like
One failure doesn't stop the rest

blocks.caption: One list, one night, a full set waiting in the morning.

community_prompts.headline: A shelf of prompts that already work.
body: The blank page is the hardest part. This is a browsable collection of prompts that are known to produce something good, each with its settings attached and a button that drops the whole thing into a generation tab, ready to run.
Use them as they are, or change three words and make them yours. New ones arrive on their own — there's nothing to update.

blocks.caption: Every one of these is one click away from being loaded and running.

gallery.headline: Everything you have made, with the recipe attached.
body: Every picture you make is kept, along with exactly how it was made. Open one from last Tuesday and you can see the prompt, the settings and the seed behind it — then run it again, or run it again with one word changed.
Browse by tab or by day, and take the lot with you in one download when you're done. Nothing is lost when you close the app.
